abstract: |
  Ultra-marginal feature importance (UMFI) credits a feature with all the predictive information it carries about a response, including information that correlated features also carry. The reference code of its linear-regression variant, UMFI-LR, removes dependence between features using all rows and scores a fixed tree ensemble by out-of-bag error. `sharedimp` provides UMFI-LR as a cross-validated procedure in R (tidymodels) and Python (scikit-learn): dependence removal is fitted inside each training split, the models with and without a feature are scored on the same held-out rows, and learner, metric and splits are chosen by the user. Both packages implement one written specification and, for learners with a unique solution, agreed within pre-specified numerical tolerances.

# Motivation and significance

Feature importance measures differ in how they treat predictive information that several features share. Permutation importance [@breiman2001random] is distorted by correlation between features, and conditional variants [@strobl2008conditional] ask what a feature adds given the others, so that a feature whose information is also available elsewhere receives little or no credit. That is appropriate for explaining a model or selecting features. When the aim is to describe relationships in the data, marginal contribution feature importance [@catav2021marginal] and ultra-marginal feature importance (UMFI) [@janssen2023umfi] take the opposite position and count shared information towards every feature that carries it.

UMFI is defined for a feature of interest $x_i$ (the *anchor*) as $\nu(S_i \cup \{x_i\}) - \nu(S_i)$, where $S_i$ is a version of the other features from which the dependence on $x_i$ has been removed and $\nu$ evaluates how well a set of features predicts the response [@janssen2023umfi]. The definition is a framework: it admits any dependence removal and any evaluation function. In the linear-regression variant, UMFI-LR, every other feature is replaced by the residual of its simple regression on the anchor.

The reference implementations of UMFI-LR, an R package and a Python module [@umfi_r; @umfi_python], fix these choices as in the experiments of the original article. We read their source at fixed commits and executed it (Section \ref{sec:official}). The regressions are estimated on all rows; $\nu$ is the out-of-bag $R^2$ or accuracy of a forest of 100 trees fitted on all rows; a feature is residualized only if a dependence test passes, and the R and Python codes use different tests; negative scores and importances are set to zero; and randomness comes from the global generator. An analyst who has already chosen a model class, a loss and a validation design for a study therefore cannot use them for the importance, and preprocessing that is estimated on the rows used for evaluation is a known source of optimistic estimates [@kaufman2012leakage].

`sharedimp` implements UMFI-LR as an ordinary resampling procedure in tidymodels [@tidymodels] and scikit-learn [@pedregosa2011scikit]. It proposes no new importance measure, and properties that follow from the definition of UMFI-LR are not findings of this software. What it adds is engineering: (i) the dependence removal is fitted on the training rows of every split and applied unchanged to the held-out rows; (ii) the models with and without the anchor are scored on the same held-out rows; (iii) learner, metric and splits are arguments; (iv) results are signed and kept per split; and (v) the two packages follow one written specification and are checked against each other. The reported quantities are out-of-sample predictive gains. They are not causal or conditional effects, and no confidence intervals or tests are provided.

# Software description

## Software architecture

Each package is a thin layer over the modelling interfaces of its ecosystem and has the same four components (Figure \ref{fig:overview}): validation of the inputs and construction of the splits (rsample; scikit-learn splitters); the residualizer, which is fitted on one set of rows and applied to another (`residualize_fit()` and `residualize_apply()` in R, the transformer `AnchorResidualizer` in Python); adapters that fit the learner and compute the metric (parsnip and yardstick; estimators and scorers); and a result object. Both implement a common specification kept with the R package (`docs/specification.md`), which defines inputs, computation, degenerate cases, metrics and result tables.

```{r overview, fig.cap="Inputs of \\texttt{shared\\_importance()} and the objects that carry them in each package (top), the computation for one anchor feature and one split (dashed frame), and the result."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("07_software_overview"))
```

For a split into training rows $T$ and assessment rows $A$ and an anchor $x_i$, every other feature $x_j$ is regressed on $x_i$ by least squares on the rows in $T$,
$$(\hat a_j, \hat b_j) = \arg\min_{a,b} \sum_{t \in T} (x_{tj} - a - b\,x_{ti})^2, \qquad r_j = x_j - \hat a_j - \hat b_j x_i ,$$
and the residual $r_j$ is computed with these coefficients for the rows in $T$ and in $A$. The *Full* representation consists of $x_i$ and the residuals, the *Reduced* representation of the residuals only. The same learner is fitted to each on $T$, giving $\hat f^{\mathrm{F}}_T$ and $\hat f^{\mathrm{R}}_T$, and the importance of $x_i$ in the split is
$$I_{T,A}(x_i) = m\bigl(\hat f^{\mathrm{F}}_T; A\bigr) - m\bigl(\hat f^{\mathrm{R}}_T; A\bigr),$$
where $m$ is the metric on the assessment rows, oriented so that larger is better. The reported importance is the mean over splits; the between-split standard deviation is a description, not a standard error. One call fits the learner $2pv$ times for $p$ features and $v$ splits.

Two consequences of this definition help in reading the results. The Full representation is an invertible affine transformation of the original features, so a linear learner with an intercept attains the same Full score for every anchor, namely its ordinary cross-validated score (the Full scores of the least-squares examples below differ between anchors by at most `r num("full_range_ols", max(c(exact_perf$full_score_range_over_anchors_r, exact_perf$full_score_range_over_anchors_python)), "results/summary/04_real_data/performance.csv", how = "sci")`). And because the residuals are uncorrelated with the anchor on the training rows, the least-squares importance under squared error estimates the variance of the response explained by the anchor alone: with a linear learner, UMFI-LR is a marginal measure evaluated out of sample.

The specification fixes the points on which two implementations would otherwise drift apart. The residualization is always applied, without a dependence test. A constant anchor and exactly collinear features are handled by deterministic rules, without injected noise and without dropping columns. Common metric names have one definition (`r2` is $1 - SS_{\mathrm{res}}/SS_{\mathrm{tot}}$ on the assessment rows, not a squared correlation), and the result tables have the same columns.

## Software functionalities

**Tasks.** Regression, binary and multiclass classification; numeric features without missing values. **Learners.** R: built-in `"linear"` (least squares, logistic or multinomial logistic regression) and `"rand_forest"` (ranger [@wright2017ranger], 500 trees), any parsnip model specification, or a pair of fit and predict functions. Python: any scikit-learn estimator or pipeline. Hyperparameters are fixed; nothing is tuned. **Metrics.** Common names (`mse`, `rmse`, `mae`, `r2`, `log_loss`, `accuracy`, `roc_auc`), any yardstick metric, any scikit-learn scorer; the importance is positive when the anchor improves prediction, for metrics to be maximized and minimized alike. **Resampling.** $v$-fold cross-validation (stratified for classification), repeats, or explicit splits, including grouped ones; the same splits serve every anchor and both models. **Results.** A summary table (`feature`, `importance`, `importance_std`, `score_full`, `score_reduced`, `n_splits`) and a per-split table, with the same columns in both languages; negative values are kept. **Robustness.** A failed model fit is recorded for its split or, on request, stops the call; a seed fixes splits and learners. Each package has a unit-test suite run by continuous integration, which also builds and publishes a container image.

Table \ref{tab:official} compares the design with the reference implementations, including what they offer and `sharedimp` does not.

## Sample code snippets

The packages are installed from GitHub. The listings run the same analysis in both languages, with a learner that has a unique solution and explicit splits (`fold` holds one label per row), so that the results can be compared.

```r
# install: pak::pak("dsc-chiba-u/sharedimp-r")
res <- sharedimp::shared_importance(x, y, learner = "linear",
                                    metric = "rmse", resamples = fold)
res$importance                  # one row per feature
sharedimp::fold_results(res)    # one row per feature and split
```

```python
# install: pip install git+https://github.com/dsc-chiba-u/sharedimp-py.git
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import PredefinedSplit
from sharedimp import shared_importance
res = shared_importance(LinearRegression(), X, y, cv=PredefinedSplit(fold),
                        scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
res.importances, res.fold_results
```

## Comparison with the reference implementations {#sec:official}

Three reference codes were fetched at fixed commits and run unmodified: the R package [@umfi_r], the original R script of the method's authors and the Python module [@umfi_python]. Numerical identity with `sharedimp` cannot be expected in general because the procedures differ (Table \ref{tab:official}); equality was tested where they coincide. For feature pairs on which the reference dependence test passes, the residual columns agree to rounding error (Table \ref{tab:validation}). Where it fails, the reference code keeps the raw column and `sharedimp` residualizes; the two reference codes themselves disagree on `r num("gate_disagree", sum(gate$gate_fired.official_r != gate$gate_fired.official_py), "results/summary/03_official_umfi/residualization.csv", how = "int")` of `r num("gate_pairs", nrow(gate), "results/summary/03_official_umfi/residualization.csv", how = "int")` feature pairs because their tests differ. On a data set on which every test passes, the reference importance equals the reference scoring rule applied to the representation that `sharedimp` builds from all rows (same seed and order of fits); on a data set on which some tests fail, the two differ by up to `r num("b3_diff", max(ic_diff$max_abs_diff_official_vs_rule_on_sharedimp), "results/summary/03_official_umfi/identical_condition.csv", digits = 3)`. The residualization arithmetic is therefore the same, and the remaining differences are differences of procedure.

How much the procedures matter depends on the setting. On the four simulation designs shipped with the reference Python code ($n = 500$, `r num("b4_seeds", unique(bd$n_seeds), "results/summary/03_official_umfi/importance_by_design.csv", how = "int")` data sets each), the mean importances of the reference R package and of `sharedimp` with its R forest and five-fold cross-validation differed by at most `r num("b4_maxdiff", max(abs(bdw$mean.x - bdw$mean.y)), "results/summary/03_official_umfi/importance_by_design.csv", digits = 3)` in $R^2$. When the response is independent of the features, every reference importance is exactly zero because of the floors, whereas `sharedimp` with least squares returns a mean of `r num("b6_ols", negv("sharedimp_r/linear", "mean"), "results/summary/03_official_umfi/negative_importance.csv", digits = 3)` in $R^2$ with `r num("b6_ols_neg", negv("sharedimp_r/linear", "share_negative"), "results/summary/03_official_umfi/negative_importance.csv", digits = 0, how = "pct")` of the values negative, as expected for a model with one superfluous coefficient.

## Effect of fold-internal residualization {#sec:leak}

To isolate the effect of the rows used for the residualization, we simulated a linear model with five correlated Gaussian features, for which the large-sample importance under squared error has a closed form, and compared procedures that differ in one step only: residualization fitted on the training rows of each split (`sharedimp`), or on all rows before the same five-fold cross-validation with the same learner (least squares) and metric (Figure \ref{fig:leak}; `r num("leak_seeds", unique(leak$n_seeds), leak_src, how = "int")` data sets per sample size). This is not a measurement of the reference implementations, which score out of bag. Residualizing on all rows raised the importance of the four informative features by `r num("leak30", leak_rel(30), leak_src, digits = 0, how = "pct")` on average at $n = 30$, `r num("leak60", leak_rel(60), leak_src, digits = 0, how = "pct")` at $n = 60$, `r num("leak120", leak_rel(120), leak_src, digits = 0, how = "pct")` at $n = 120$ and `r num("leak2000", leak_rel(2000), leak_src, digits = 1, how = "pct")` at $n = 2000$ (with the preprocessing function of the reference R package, which includes its dependence test, in place of the all-rows residualization: `r num("leak30_gate", leak_gate_rel(30), leak_src, digits = 0, how = "pct")` at $n = 30$). The fold-internal means deviated from the large-sample values by at most `r num("leak_fold_dev", max(abs(leak_inf$fold_internal - leak_inf$population) / leak_inf$population), leak_src, digits = 0, how = "pct")`, without a common sign (first feature, $n = 30$: `r num("leak30_x1_fold", lk(30, "x1", "fold_internal"), leak_src, digits = 2)` fold-internal, `r num("leak30_x1_all", lk(30, "x1", "all_rows"), leak_src, digits = 2)` all rows, large-sample value `r num("leak_x1_pop", lk(30, "x1", "population"), leak_src, digits = 0)`).

The feature $x_4$ is independent of the response and of the other features, and shows the price of residualizing unconditionally. Its fold-internal importance is positive in small samples (`r num("leak30_x4_fold", lk(30, "x4", "fold_internal"), leak_src, digits = 2)` at $n = 30$, `r num("leak120_x4_fold", lk(120, "x4", "fold_internal"), leak_src, digits = 2)` at $n = 120$, `r num("leak2000_x4_fold", lk(2000, "x4", "fold_internal"), leak_src, digits = 3)` at $n = 2000$): slopes that are zero in the population are estimated with error, so the Reduced representation lacks a small part of the informative features that the Full model recovers through the anchor. The reference dependence test, which leaves a feature untouched unless its slope is significant, largely avoids this (`r num("leak30_x4_gate", lk(30, "x4", "all_rows_official_gate"), leak_src, digits = 2)` at $n = 30$). Both effects are small-sample effects and were measured with least squares only.

```{r leak, fig.cap="Importance (reduction in mean squared error) of five features of a linear Gaussian model against the sample size, by the rows on which the residualization is fitted; least squares and the same five-fold cross-validation throughout. Means over simulated data sets; bars: $\\pm 2$ Monte Carlo standard errors (fold-internal only); dashed: large-sample value. $x_4$ is unrelated to the response and to the other features."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("07_fold_internal_effect"))
```

## Agreement between R and Python {#sec:parity}

Both packages were run on the same data files with the same fold labels and metrics, and every numeric column of both result tables was compared (Table \ref{tab:validation}). The largest difference is at rounding level for least squares and below the tolerances fixed in advance for binary and multinomial logistic regression, where the two languages use different iterative optimisers and agreement is limited by their convergence. The claim is restricted in three ways. It concerns learners with a unique solution on full-rank designs: when a training design is rank-deficient, least-squares solvers that are each correct can predict differently on new rows, and the packages pass the representations to the learner as given. It does not extend to random forests: ranger and scikit-learn define their node-size parameters differently and count node sizes differently under bootstrap sampling, so equal settings do not give equal trees, and forest results are reported per language as usage examples. And it is a statement about the analyses that were run, not a proof for all inputs.

## Public data sets {#sec:data}

Figure \ref{fig:examples} shows three data sets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository: Concrete Compressive Strength [@uci_concrete] (regression, $n$ = `r num("n_concrete", one(ds$n[ds$dataset == "concrete"]), "results/summary/04_real_data/datasets.csv", how = "int")`, `r num("p_concrete", as.numeric(one(ds$p[ds$dataset == "concrete"])), "results/summary/04_real_data/datasets.csv", how = "int")` features), the ten mean features of Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic) [@uci_wdbc] (binary, $n$ = `r num("n_wdbc", one(ds$n[ds$dataset == "wdbc"]), "results/summary/04_real_data/datasets.csv", how = "int")`) and Maternal Health Risk [@uci_maternal] (three classes, $n$ = `r num("n_maternal", one(ds$n[ds$dataset == "maternal"]), "results/summary/04_real_data/datasets.csv", how = "int")`, `r num("p_maternal", as.numeric(one(ds$p[ds$dataset == "maternal"])), "results/summary/04_real_data/datasets.csv", how = "int")` features), each with a linear and a forest learner and five folds. The cross-validated $R^2$ of the Full model on Concrete is `r num("concrete_r2_lin", pf("concrete_linear_r2", "full_score_r"), "results/summary/04_real_data/performance.csv", digits = 3)` with least squares and `r num("concrete_r2_rf_r", pf("concrete_rf_r2", "full_score_r"), "results/summary/04_real_data/performance.csv", digits = 3)` with the R forest; the log-loss on Breast Cancer is `r num("wdbc_ll_lin", -pf("wdbc_linear_logloss", "full_score_r"), "results/summary/04_real_data/performance.csv", digits = 3)` with logistic regression. Several forest importances on Concrete are negative in both languages: the model with the anchor predicted worse than the model without it, which truncation at zero would hide.

```{r examples, fig.cap="Importances (mean and standard deviation over five splits) on three public data sets. Left: least squares, logistic and multinomial logistic regression, which agree between R and Python within the tolerances of Table \\ref{tab:validation}. Right: random forests with language-specific settings, not expected to agree. For Maternal Health Risk the folds keep rows with identical feature values together."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("07_examples_importance"))
```

The Maternal Health Risk file required a decision about the validation design. Of its `r num("mat_rows", dup$rows, "results/raw/04b_maternal/duplicates.json", how = "int")` rows only `r num("mat_distinct", dup$identical_record$distinct_records, "results/raw/04b_maternal/duplicates.json", how = "int")` are distinct records; `r num("mat_repeat", dup$identical_record$rows_that_repeat_an_earlier_record, "results/raw/04b_maternal/duplicates.json", how = "int")` rows repeat an earlier row in all features and the label. The origin of the repeated rows is unknown: the provider's documentation does not say whether they are repeated observations or copies. With random folds, `r num("mat_leak", dup$random_folds_of_experiment_C$assessment_rows_whose_feature_vector_is_also_in_the_training_rows, "results/raw/04b_maternal/duplicates.json", how = "int")` assessment rows have their feature values among the training rows, and the performance estimate is optimistic for a learner that can memorize rows: the R forest reaches a log-loss of `r num("mat_rf_random", ms("rand_forest", "log_loss", "r", "maternal"), "results/summary/04b_maternal/scores.csv", digits = 3)` against `r num("mat_lin_random", ms("linear", "log_loss", "r", "maternal"), "results/summary/04b_maternal/scores.csv", digits = 3)` for the multinomial model. The main analysis therefore keeps all rows and uses group-aware folds, in which rows with identical feature values share a fold; it needs no assumption about what the repeated rows are. There the forest has no advantage (`r num("mat_rf_grouped", ms("rand_forest", "log_loss", "r", "maternal_grouped"), "results/summary/04b_maternal/scores.csv", digits = 3)` against `r num("mat_lin_grouped", ms("linear", "log_loss", "r", "maternal_grouped"), "results/summary/04b_maternal/scores.csv", digits = 3)`), while the importances of the multinomial model hardly change (largest change `r num("mat_change", max(mrank$largest_abs_change_of_importance[mrank$learner == "linear" & mrank$metric == "log_loss" & mrank$variant == "maternal_grouped"]), "results/summary/04b_maternal/rank_agreement.csv", digits = 3)`). As a sensitivity analysis, removing identical records (`r num("mat_dedup_n", one(mvar$rows[mvar$variant == "maternal_dedup"]), "results/summary/04b_maternal/variants.csv", how = "int")` rows) gives `r num("mat_lin_dedup", ms("linear", "log_loss", "r", "maternal_dedup"), "results/summary/04b_maternal/scores.csv", digits = 3)` for the multinomial model and `r num("mat_rf_dedup", ms("rand_forest", "log_loss", "r", "maternal_dedup"), "results/summary/04b_maternal/scores.csv", digits = 3)` for the forest; this is the appropriate analysis only if the repeated rows are copies. Blood sugar ranks first in all three analyses. We screened `r num("sel_n", nrow(sel), "results/summary/04a_multiclass_pilot/decision.csv", how = "int")` other public multiclass data sets against criteria fixed beforehand; none met all of them, so this data set was kept, and it should be read as an illustration of the software, not as a clinical analysis.

## Runtime

Single calls were timed on one thread of an `r reg("cpu", sub("\\(R\\)", "", sub("\\(R\\) Xeon\\(R\\)", " Xeon", sub(" CPU.*$", "", one(unique(rd("05_runtime", "environment.csv")$cpu))))), "results/summary/05_runtime/environment.csv")` processor, on the same machine and data files for both languages (one warm-up and five timed calls per condition; medians reported; interquartile range at most `r num("rt_iqr", max(cells$iqr[cells$status == "measured"] / cells$median[cells$status == "measured"]), cells_src, digits = 1, how = "pct")` of the median). Synthetic regression data were used, varying the number of rows $n$, features $p$ and folds $v$ one at a time around $n = 1000$, $p = 10$, $v = 5$ (Figure \ref{fig:runtime}). A budget of two hours and a rule for skipping conditions were fixed before the measurements. Of `r num("rt_cells", nrow(cells), cells_src, how = "int")` planned combinations of condition, language and learner, `r num("rt_measured", sum(cells$status == "measured"), cells_src, how = "int")` were measured: all `r num("rt_lin_all", n_all("linear"), cells_src, how = "int")` with least squares, `r num("rt_rf_meas", n_meas(c("rand_forest", "rf_aligned")), cells_src, how = "int")` of `r num("rt_rf_all", n_all(c("rand_forest", "rf_aligned")), cells_src, how = "int")` with the forests of Figure \ref{fig:runtime}, and `r num("rt_cust_meas", n_meas("rf_customary"), cells_src, how = "int")` of `r num("rt_cust_all", n_all("rf_customary"), cells_src, how = "int")` with scikit-learn's default forest (reported in the repository). Forest runtime is therefore known only for $n \le 1000$, $p \le 10$ and $v \le 5$.

With least squares the base condition took `r num("rt_lin_r", rt("A_linear", 1000, 10, 5, "r_median"), rt_src, digits = 2)` s in R and `r num("rt_lin_py", rt("A_linear", 1000, 10, 5, "python_median"), rt_src, digits = 2)` s in Python, and `r num("rt_lin_r_p160", rt("A_linear", 1000, 160, 5, "r_median"), rt_src, digits = 1)` s and `r num("rt_lin_py_p160", rt("A_linear", 1000, 160, 5, "python_median"), rt_src, digits = 1)` s with 160 features (1600 model fits); up to $n = 1000$ the time hardly depended on $n$, the fixed cost of a model fit being dominant, and at $n = 32000$ the Python call was the faster one (`r num("rt_lin_py_n32000", rt("A_linear", 32000, 10, 5, "python_median"), rt_src, digits = 2)` s against `r num("rt_lin_r_n32000", rt("A_linear", 32000, 10, 5, "r_median"), rt_src, digits = 2)` s). With the R built-in forest the base condition took `r num("rt_rf_r", rt("B_forest_aligned", 1000, 10, 5, "r_median"), rt_src, digits = 1)` s, and `r num("rt_rf_py", rt("B_forest_aligned", 1000, 10, 5, "python_median"), rt_src, digits = 1)` s with a scikit-learn forest of 500 trees whose settings have the same definitions but which is not the same learner. The number of model fits, $2pv$, follows from the algorithm and was confirmed by counting (Table \ref{tab:validation}); the time per fit belongs to the learner. The timings include differences between the learner implementations and linear-algebra libraries of the two environments. They do not rank the languages, and no order of growth is inferred from them.

```{r runtime, fig.cap="Wall-clock time of one call of \\texttt{shared\\_importance()} on one thread against the number of rows, features and folds, one factor varied at a time. Top: least squares. Bottom: random forests of 500 trees with settings of the same definition in ranger (R) and scikit-learn (Python). Conditions excluded by the time budget are absent."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("07_runtime"))
```

# Impact

## What was difficult and is now direct

With the reference code, a UMFI-LR analysis is tied to a forest scored out of bag. Three things that applied analyses routinely need were therefore unavailable without rewriting the procedure, and are arguments in `sharedimp`. The first is the validation design. Out-of-bag scoring resamples rows and has no notion of groups, blocks or repeated measurements, whereas `sharedimp` accepts the splits that the design requires; in the Maternal Health Risk example, ignoring the repeated rows changed the apparent quality of the forest from a log-loss of `r num("mat_rf_grouped", ms("rand_forest", "log_loss", "r", "maternal_grouped"), "results/summary/04b_maternal/scores.csv", digits = 3)` to `r num("mat_rf_random", ms("rand_forest", "log_loss", "r", "maternal"), "results/summary/04b_maternal/scores.csv", digits = 3)`. The second is the model class and the loss of the study: a penalized regression, a boosting model or a pipeline, scored by a probability metric, can be passed as it is, so that the importance refers to the same model and the same loss as the performance reported next to it. The third is the sign and the spread: per-split, untruncated values show when a model with the feature predicted worse on new rows.

## Research questions and settings

UMFI addresses analyses whose aim is to learn from data, where correlated measurements are the rule [@janssen2023umfi]. Because the dependence removal is part of the resampling loop, `sharedimp` turns the question "does this measurement carry predictive information about the outcome, whether or not other measurements carry it too?" into an out-of-sample statement for a named model class, metric and validation design. This matters most in small samples, the setting in which fitting the residualization on all rows inflated the cross-validated importances in our simulation (Section \ref{sec:leak}). The software also makes methodological questions about UMFI-LR itself easy to pose, such as its dependence on the learner, its behaviour for uninformative features, or the effect of the dependence test, because each of these is one argument or one exported function away. The packages are released with this article, and we make no claim about their adoption.

## Reproducible analyses in two languages

Groups that mix R and Python can run the same analysis in either language. For learners with a unique solution the two packages returned the same result tables within the tolerances of Table \ref{tab:validation}, so a result can be recomputed with an independent implementation, a check that a single-language package cannot offer. This rests on a written specification with executable checks, not on a port: the specification names every case in which the implementations had to make the same choice, and the comparison on identical data and splits is part of the public record, together with the container images in which it was run.

## Limitations

Only the linear-regression variant is implemented. Dependence that is not linear in the anchor remains in the representation, and the original article reports a data set on which linear regression failed to remove it [@janssen2023umfi]; features must be numeric and complete. Residualizing unconditionally gives features unrelated to the others a positive importance in small samples (Section \ref{sec:leak}). The estimates are signed and no evaluation function is forced to be non-negative, so the guarantees proved in the original article for an idealized evaluation function are not claimed for them; they are descriptive, without intervals or tests, and one five-fold split per data set was used in the examples. Agreement between the languages is established for learners with a unique solution on full-rank designs only (Section \ref{sec:parity}), and for a thresholded metric such as accuracy one observation with nearly tied class probabilities can be classified differently although the fitted probabilities agree (observed once, on a candidate data set, with probabilities agreeing within `r num("flip_prob", one(rd("04a_multiclass_pilot", "flips.csv")$largest_abs_probability_difference), "results/summary/04a_multiclass_pilot/flips.csv", how = "sci")`). With flexible learners the importance under a response independent of the features is not centred at zero, because the two models differ in their number of columns: in a small simulation its mean was `r num("null_r", nf("r", "null_p5", "baseline"), "results/summary/04c_null_forest/summary.csv", digits = 3)` in $R^2$ for the R built-in forest with five features, and `r num("null_r_padded", nf("r", "null_p5", "padded_reduced"), "results/summary/04c_null_forest/summary.csv", digits = 3)` when both models had the same number of columns, so small positive forest importances should not be read as evidence of information. Finally, the cost is $2pv$ model fits, and forest runtime was measured for small problems only.

# Conclusions

`sharedimp` provides UMFI-LR as a resampling procedure in R and in Python. It does not alter the definition of the measure; it changes how the measure is estimated and delivered: residualization inside each training split, paired scoring on held-out rows, free choice of learner, metric and splits, signed per-split results, and two implementations bound by one specification that are checked against each other and, where the procedures coincide, against the reference code.

# Reproducibility and data availability {#sec:repro .unnumbered}

The experiments, their configuration, the recorded results and the source of this manuscript are in \url{https://github.com/dsc-chiba-u/sharedimp-experiments}. The workflows run with Snakemake `r reg("snakemake", envv("host", "Snakemake"), "results/summary/01_environment/environment.csv")` [@molder2021snakemake] and Singularity `r reg("singularity", sub("^singularity version ", "", envv("host", "Singularity")), "results/summary/01_environment/environment.csv")` [@kurtzer2017singularity] inside container images pinned by digest; every number in this article is read from the recorded results when the manuscript is built. The reference UMFI code is not redistributed; it is fetched at the cited commits when the comparison is run. No new data were collected: the three public data sets are available from the UCI Machine Learning Repository under CC BY 4.0, and the prepared files, their checksums and the simulated data are in the repository.
